title: Process priority & lifecycle
scopeHtml: Scope: how Android ranks and kills app processes (importance classes, oom_adj, lmkd), what keeps a process alive, Application/process start, multi-process apps, onTrimMemory and start types. Process-death state restoration is chunk 04; Doze/OEM killers are chunk 17; profiling depth is A6.

notes.title: Process importance classes
notes.html:
The idea. Your phone has limited memory. When it runs low, Android must close some apps. It does not pick randomly: it ranks every process by how much the user cares about it right now, and kills the least important first. Those ranks are the importance classes.

The ranking (most to least important).

Class Who is in it Typical oom_adj score
Foreground App with the visible, resumed Activity; a Service running onCreate/onStart/onDestroy; a BroadcastReceiver in onReceive; a foreground service holder 0
Visible Activity visible but paused (a dialog-theme Activity on top, split-screen neighbour) 100
Perceptible Playing music, a user-noticeable service 200
Service (A/B) Started service running in background 500 / 800
Cached (previous/home/empty) Stopped Activities, no components running 900 to 999

(Scores come from ProcessList in AOSP; exact values vary across versions, so confirm in source if asked.) The public API view is ActivityManager.RunningAppProcessInfo.importance with constants like IMPORTANCE_FOREGROUND, IMPORTANCE_VISIBLE, IMPORTANCE_SERVICE, IMPORTANCE_CACHED.

 killed LAST                                           killed FIRST
 [Foreground] > [Visible] > [Perceptible] > [Service] > [Cached]

Real products. Spotify and YouTube Music playing in the background keep a media foreground service with a notification, so they survive when Instagram, sitting stopped in the cache, is killed. Google Maps navigation uses a location foreground service for the same reason.

Analogy. A lifeboat with limited seats: the person speaking on stage stays, the audience in the front row stays, the people dozing at the back are asked to leave first.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "Android kills the app using the most memory". It kills by importance first; memory size is a tiebreaker inside the same class.
  • Believing a started Service keeps the process "foreground". A plain background service is only in the Service class and is subject to being killed and to background limits on API 26+.
  • Assuming the process dies when the last Activity finishes. It becomes cached and stays until the system needs memory.

notes.title: Cold, warm and hot start
notes.html:
The idea. Opening an app is slow if the system must build everything from scratch, fast if it already has pieces ready.

  • Cold start: no process exists. Zygote forks a new process, the runtime loads, Application is created, then the Activity is created and the first frame is drawn. Slowest.
  • Warm start: process alive but Activity gone (back-pressed, or destroyed while the process lives). Skips process creation and Application.onCreate, but runs Activity.onCreate again.
  • Hot start: process and Activity both in memory, only onRestart/onStart/onResume. Fastest.
Cold: fork Zygote -> bindApplication -> Application.onCreate -> Activity.onCreate
      -> onStart/onResume -> first frame (Initial Display)

Measurement. Time-to-initial-display (TTID) is logged by the system as Displayed in logcat (ActivityTaskManager: Displayed pkg/.Main: +812ms); time-to-full-display (TTFD) needs reportFullyDrawn(). Play Console Android vitals flags cold start over 5 s, warm over 2 s and hot over 1.5 s as excessive (confirm current thresholds in docs). Jetpack Macrobenchmark's StartupTimingMetric measures it in CI; Baseline Profiles typically cut cold start noticeably by precompiling hot paths (Google quotes improvements of up to about 30 percent; measure your own app). Android 12+ also shows the splash-screen window straight from the system, so users see something while cold start runs.

Real products. Swiggy, Paytm and Uber track cold-start P90 and use Baseline Profiles and lazy SDK init (App Startup library, lazy Hilt/Dagger) to stay under budget.

Analogy. Cold = opening a restaurant from scratch (lights, stove, staff). Warm = restaurant open but your table cleared, so only the table is set again. Hot = you simply return to the table you left.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking a warm start skips Activity.onCreate. It does not; only a hot start does.
  • Measuring startup in a debug build. Debug is not R8-optimised and not AOT compiled, so numbers mislead.
  • Forgetting that a user "resuming" an app after process death is in practice a cold start.

notes.title: onTrimMemory
notes.html:
The idea. Before the system kills you, it can tap you on the shoulder: "free what you can". That tap is ComponentCallbacks2.onTrimMemory(level), available in Application, Activity, Service and ContentProvider.

Levels you should know.

Constant Meaning
TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN (20) Your UI is no longer visible: drop UI-only caches (bitmaps for screens)
TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_MODERATE/LOW/CRITICAL (5/10/15) You are running and the device is short of memory
TRIM_MEMORY_BACKGROUND/MODERATE/COMPLETE (40/60/80) You are cached on the LRU list; COMPLETE means next to be killed

Several of the older constants are deprecated in recent API levels (confirm in docs), but UI_HIDDEN and the cached-level ones remain the common practice. The callback is a hint, not a promise. Under sudden pressure lmkd kills you with no callback at all.

override fun onTrimMemory(level: Int) {
    super.onTrimMemory(level)
    if (level >= ComponentCallbacks2.TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN) imageCache.trimToSize(0)
}

Real products. Glide and Coil register for trim callbacks and shrink their memory caches. Instagram-style feeds drop decoded bitmaps when the UI hides.

Analogy. A hotel announcing "checkout soon, please clear your room" before housekeeping starts removing luggage.

Common interview traps.

  • Relying on onTrimMemory or onLowMemory to save user data. Save state in onStop/ViewModel/SavedStateHandle; the kill may give no warning.
  • Freeing memory only at COMPLETE level; by then you are first in line to die.
  • Forgetting it fires per process, so a multi-process app gets callbacks in each process.

notes.title: oom_adj and lmkd
notes.html:
The idea. Each process has a score; higher score = more killable. A small daemon watches memory pressure and kills the highest-score process.

Mechanism. ActivityManagerService computes an oom_score_adj per process (see the table in the importance section) and hands it to lmkd, a native daemon that replaced the old in-kernel low-memory-killer driver (around Android 9 to 10). lmkd writes the score to /proc/<pid>/oom_score_adj. From Android 10 lmkd can use PSI (Pressure Stall Information) from the kernel: it reacts when tasks are stalling on memory, not only when free pages drop below fixed thresholds. It picks the process with the highest score (and largest among those) and sends SIGKILL.

memory pressure (PSI) up -> lmkd wakes -> pick highest oom_score_adj
  -> SIGKILL the biggest cached process -> re-check

Your process sees nothing: no finally, no onDestroy. It just ends. A line like lowmemorykiller: Kill 'pkg' (pid), uid, oom_score_adj 900 ... to free N kB appears in logcat, and since Android 11 ApplicationExitInfo reports REASON_LOW_MEMORY.

Real products. On low-RAM devices (Android Go, 2 GB phones common in India) your cached process may die within seconds of backgrounding; WhatsApp and Gmail therefore persist things to disk eagerly.

Analogy. A bouncer removing the least important guests when the room gets too crowded, without letting them finish their sentence.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing you can catch the kill (no handler can catch SIGKILL).
  • Quoting fixed MB thresholds; modern lmkd decisions are PSI-based and device-tuned.
  • Confusing Java OutOfMemoryError (your heap limit, catchable in theory) with an lmkd kill (system-wide, no catch).

notes.title: What keeps a process alive and importance propagation
notes.html:
The idea. Your process rank is the rank of the most important thing inside it, plus the ranks it inherits from clients that depend on it.

Things that raise rank.

  • A visible Activity (foreground/visible).
  • A foreground service (startForeground) and a running onReceive.
  • A bound client that is more important: if a foreground app binds to your Service, your process rises to at least that level. Bind flags matter: BIND_AUTO_CREATE creates the service; BIND_IMPORTANT pushes the service up to the client's importance; BIND_ABOVE_CLIENT and BIND_NOT_FOREGROUND modify it.
  • A ContentProvider in use by a client holds the provider's process at about the client's level through a reference.
[Foreground app A] --bindService--> [Your service process B]
B inherits A's importance while the connection is live.

Not keeping alive: a static object, a running Thread, or a pending Handler message. Threads are not components, so the system does not count them.

Real products. Android Auto binds to the media browser services of Spotify and others, lifting them while the car screen is connected. Google Play Services binds to many app services the same way.

Analogy. A plumber is "important" while the palace has him on call; his rank depends on his most important customer.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing a running thread keeps the process alive.
  • Forgetting that unbinding drops the inherited rank, causing a sudden kill of a once-safe service.
  • Saying the system never kills a process with a foreground service; extreme memory pressure still can, and Android 12+ restricts starting one from the background.

notes.title: Application.onCreate timing and cost
notes.html:
The idea. Application.onCreate runs on the main thread on every cold start, before any Activity can draw. Anything slow there is paid by every launch.

Order in a cold process (simplified). Application.attachBaseContext -> ContentProvider.onCreate of every declared provider (including library providers such as FirebaseInitProvider and androidx.startup InitializationProvider) -> Application.onCreate -> Activity. Providers run before Application.onCreate, a classic gotcha (see the ContentProviders topic).

class App : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        // BAD: blocking disk, network, a huge DI graph, parsing a 2 MB JSON
        // GOOD: only what the first screen needs; defer the rest
        Handler(Looper.getMainLooper()).post { initAnalytics() }   // or idle / background
    }
}

Cold start regression playbook.

  1. Capture a Perfetto/system trace or use the Android Studio profiler on startup; look at the bindApplication and activityStart slices.
  2. Use Macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric before and after the suspect change.
  3. Defer non-critical SDKs (App Startup library with lazy initializers, Lazy<> in Hilt, by lazy).
  4. Move disk/network off the main thread; avoid big SharedPreferences reads or commit() in onCreate.
  5. Add Baseline Profiles; check for a new dependency adding provider-based auto-init, reflection or MultiDex.
  6. Run with StrictMode to catch accidental disk/network on main.

A frequent regression source: someone adds an analytics, ads or crash SDK that initialises eagerly via its own provider, adding tens to hundreds of ms.

Real products. Uber and Meta engineering blogs describe startup budgets and startup-task dependency graphs. Firebase's auto-init through FirebaseInitProvider is the well-known provider-based example.

Analogy. A shop where the owner must sort all stock, call every supplier and mop the whole floor before unlocking the door each morning.

Common interview traps.

  • Moving work to a background thread but then waiting for it on the main thread.
  • Assuming Application.onCreate runs once per app; it runs once per process.
  • Optimising Activity layout while ignoring providers that run before Application.onCreate.

notes.title: Multi-process apps
notes.html:
The idea. One app can run components in several OS processes using android:process in the manifest. Each process has its own memory, its own copy of every static variable, its own Application object and its own runtime.

<service android:name=".SyncService" android:process=":sync" />
<activity android:name=".WebAuthActivity" android:process=":web" />

:name makes a process private to the app; a name without the colon is a global process that can be shared with apps using the same user id/signature.

Why use it.

  • Crash isolation: a crash (including native) in :web or :player does not kill the main UI process.
  • Memory: a heavy component can be killed independently, and each process has its own heap limit.
  • Sandboxing: isolatedProcess="true" services run with no permissions.

Costs.

  • Every process runs Application.onCreate again, plus tens of MB extra RSS.
  • Singletons and in-memory caches are not shared. Moving data needs IPC: Binder/AIDL, Messenger, a ContentProvider, files, or broadcasts. SharedPreferences is not multi-process safe (MODE_MULTI_PROCESS is deprecated). Room offers enableMultiInstanceInvalidation(); DataStore has a separate multi-process factory (confirm in docs).
  • Debugging and testing are harder.

Production incident (per-process Application). An analytics, DI or WorkManager init in Application.onCreate also runs in :sync, duplicating a network call or opening a database twice; users see double notifications or SQLiteDatabaseLockedException. Fix: check the process name (Application.getProcessName() on API 28+; ActivityManager or /proc/self/cmdline earlier) and init only what that process needs.

override fun onCreate() {
    super.onCreate()
    if (Application.getProcessName() == packageName) initMain() else initLight()
}

WebView in a second process (spot-the-bug). From API 28 only one process per app may use a given WebView data directory. A second process that creates a WebView without calling WebView.setDataDirectorySuffix("web") first crashes with a RuntimeException saying WebView from more than one process with the same data directory is not supported. Fix: call setDataDirectorySuffix before the first WebView use in that process.

Design trade-off. Split a process only when you can name the concrete benefit (crash isolation for a video player, keeping a heavy SDK away from the UI). Otherwise memory, startup and IPC costs outweigh it.

Real products. Chrome uses separate renderer processes; many apps with a push SDK put it in a :push process; WebView renderers are sandboxed processes.

Analogy. Two kitchens in one restaurant: a fire in one does not burn the other, but each needs its own staff, fridge and recipe copy, and sharing anything means shouting through the wall.

Common interview traps.

  • Using a Kotlin object/static as shared state across processes.
  • Not guarding Application.onCreate init by process name.
  • Using SharedPreferences for cross-process flags.
  • Forgetting the WebView data-directory suffix on API 28+.

notes.title: App standby buckets (brief)
notes.html:
The idea. From Android 9 (API 28) the system sorts apps by how recently and often the user uses them, and throttles background work for rarely used ones.

Bucket Meaning Rough effect
Active Used right now essentially none
Working set Used often jobs and alarms deferred up to about 2 h
Frequent Used regularly, not daily up to about 8 h
Rare Rarely used up to about 24 h; FCM high-priority quota limited
Restricted Battery-abusing or user-restricted roughly one job a day, tight limits
Never Installed, never opened cannot run jobs

(Intervals are approximate; confirm in docs.) Buckets affect JobScheduler/WorkManager, alarms, and FCM high-priority message quota. Check with adb shell am get-standby-bucket <pkg>; test with adb shell am set-standby-bucket <pkg> rare.

Real products. A food-delivery app opened twice a month sits in Rare, so periodic sync is delayed; apps like Swiggy therefore rely on FCM and refresh-on-launch rather than constant polling.

Analogy. A library that lets regular members borrow anytime but makes occasional visitors queue.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting a PeriodicWorkRequest to run at exact times regardless of bucket.
  • Thinking buckets only apply during Doze; they apply always.

notes.title: Deaths that are not low-memory kills and ApplicationExitInfo
notes.html:
The idea. A process vanishing is not always lmkd. Many things end it, and since Android 11 (API 30) you can ask why.

ActivityManager.getHistoricalProcessExitReasons(pkg, pid, max) returns ApplicationExitInfo records. Useful reason values:

Reason Cause
REASON_LOW_MEMORY lmkd killed it
REASON_ANR ANR kill
REASON_CRASH / REASON_CRASH_NATIVE uncaught Java exception / native crash
REASON_EXCESSIVE_RESOURCE_USAGE resource abuse
REASON_USER_REQUESTED user force-stopped or similar
REASON_USER_STOPPED user/profile stopped
REASON_PERMISSION_CHANGE permission change restarted the app
REASON_DEPENDENCY_DIED a process it depended on died
REASON_SIGNALED, REASON_INITIALIZATION_FAILURE, REASON_OTHER misc

getTraceInputStream() can give the ANR trace for REASON_ANR. Log the last exit reason on next start and attach it to Crashlytics custom keys; this is how teams find "silent" kills that never produce a crash report.

val am = getSystemService(ActivityManager::class.java)
am.getHistoricalProcessExitReasons(packageName, 0, 5).forEach {
    log("exit ${it.reason} ${it.description} importance=${it.importance}")
}

Other non-memory deaths: force-stop from Settings (kills everything, cancels alarms, blocks broadcasts until the user opens the app again), revoking some runtime permissions, your own Process.killProcess, native crashes, an FGS that failed to call startForeground in time, and OEM battery managers (Xiaomi, Oppo, Vivo, Huawei) killing aggressively.

Real products. Sentry and Crashlytics-based setups read exit info to classify ANRs and OOM-like kills.

Analogy. A missing student: sick (crash), expelled (permission), picked up by parents (user swipe), or sent out of a crowded classroom (memory). The attendance register (exit info) says which.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting a crash report for lmkd or force-stop kills; there is none.
  • Assuming exit info exists below API 30.
  • Forgetting that after force-stop no component runs until the user opens the app manually.

notes.title: Cached app freezer and phantom process limit
notes.html:
The idea. Modern Android does not only kill cached apps; it can freeze them so they use no CPU while staying in RAM, and it limits child processes.

  • Cached app freezer: introduced experimentally in Android 11 and enabled on many Android 12+ devices. A cached process with no active work is frozen via the cgroup freezer after a short delay. While frozen it gets no CPU: no timers, no wake-ups, no Handler messages. Sync Binder calls into a frozen process can cause problems, so the system unfreezes on incoming work (confirm details in docs).
  • Phantom process limit (Android 12 and later): the system caps child native (forked) processes of all apps at 32 by default. Beyond that the oldest phantom processes are killed with SIGKILL, visible as signal 9 and REASON_SIGNALED. It hits apps that fork many native helpers, such as terminal emulators like Termux. Developers can disable the monitor in Developer options or with an adb setting, but you cannot ask end users to.

Practical impact. Do not rely on a cached process doing timer-based work; use WorkManager, JobScheduler or a foreground service. Handler.postDelayed, Thread.sleep loops and Timers freeze with the process.

Analogy. Freezing is putting the app in a freezer: not thrown away, but it can do nothing until the user returns. Killing is throwing it away.

Common interview traps.

  • Counting on a background Timer to fire for a cached app.
  • Confusing freezer (stops CPU) with kill (frees memory).
  • Not knowing the 32 phantom-process cap when asked why a forking app dies.

notes.title: Staying alive in background and background kill during work
notes.html:
The idea. The honest answer to "how do I keep my app alive forever?" is: you cannot, and should not. You design for being killed.

Scenario: a large video upload dies mid-way. Root cause: a plain thread or started service in a background process dies when the process is cached and killed. Fixes, in order of preference:

  1. WorkManager (expedited, or a long-running CoroutineWorker calling setForeground(ForegroundInfo)) for user-visible work; it is persisted, retried and survives process death.
  2. A foreground service with the correct Android 14 type (dataSync, mediaPlayback, location ...) and a notification, for work the user knows about.
  3. Persist progress (chunk offsets) so a retry resumes instead of restarting.
  4. For server-driven wake-ups use FCM high priority; for exact times use alarm APIs only with a justified permission.

Ambiguous requirement ("keep the app running in the background"). Ask what is really needed: location tracking, music, chat delivery, or periodic sync? Each has a sanctioned mechanism. Anti-patterns: fake silent audio, restarting a service from onDestroy, relying on START_STICKY alone, and asking for battery-optimisation exemption (Google Play restricts that permission to certain use cases). OEM auto-start lists still kill despite everything; dontkillmyapp.com documents the vendors.

Real products. WhatsApp relies on FCM for message arrival, Uber uses a location foreground service during a trip, Google Photos uses WorkManager for backup, and Strava uses a foreground location service while recording.

Analogy. Do not try to make the shop never close; keep the ledger so that when the shutters come down, tomorrow's staff continue from the last entry.

Common interview traps.

  • Offering START_STICKY as the complete answer (it restarts with a null intent after a delay and not after force-stop).
  • Keeping state only in memory (Activity, ViewModel or service fields).
  • Suggesting wake locks to prevent kills; they stop CPU sleep, not lmkd.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Processes are ranked foreground > visible > perceptible > service > cached; lmkd kills the highest oom_score_adj first, using PSI on modern versions.
  • Cold, warm and hot start differ in whether the process and Activity exist; Application.onCreate and providers cost every cold start and every extra process.
  • onTrimMemory is a hint; the kill itself gives no callback. Persist state early.
  • Rank comes from the best component inside plus the clients bound to you; threads alone do not keep you alive.
  • Extra processes give crash isolation but duplicate Application init, break in-memory sharing and need IPC and a WebView directory suffix.
  • Standby buckets, the cached app freezer and the phantom process cap all limit background work; ApplicationExitInfo (API 30) tells you why you died.
  • Design for death: WorkManager, foreground service with the right type, persisted progress.

questions.promptHtml: What are the process importance classes in Android, and how does the system decide which class your app's process is in?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tells me whether you understand that the OS ranks processes, not apps or Activities, and that "my app is in background" is not one state.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Android keeps one process per app by default and ranks it by the most important component running inside it. The classes, from most to least protected, are foreground, visible, service, and cached. A process with a resumed Activity or a running foreground service is foreground. One with a visible but not focused Activity is visible. One with only started or bound services is service. One with nothing user-relevant is cached and is the first to be killed when memory is short. The rank is recomputed continuously, and the highest-ranked component wins.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The unit of ranking is the process, because memory is reclaimed by killing processes. ActivityManagerService (AMS) walks every component in the process and computes an importance (internally oom_adj / oom_score_adj, see Q094). The process takes the best (lowest) value among its components.

Class        What puts you here                                   Killed when
-----------  ---------------------------------------------------  ---------------------
Foreground   Resumed Activity (user is interacting)               Almost never; only
             Foreground service (startForeground)                 under critical
             Service in onCreate/onStart/onDestroy                pressure
             BroadcastReceiver in onReceive
             Provider/service bound to a foreground client
Visible      Activity visible but paused (dialog/translucent      Only to keep
             Activity on top, multi-window not focused)           foreground alive
             Service bound to a visible client
Service      startService() service that is running               When memory is
             (not foreground)                                     tight, after cached
Cached       Stopped Activities, no active components             First, in LRU order
             (LRU list; "empty" processes are the same idea)

Key mechanics:

  • A process is not "foreground" because the app feels active. It is foreground because a component in it is in a specific state right now.
  • Importance propagates through dependencies: a service bound by a foreground Activity is ranked as high as that client (see Q104).
  • Moving to cached does not mean the process dies. It means it is first in line. A cached process still holds your singletons and static state until it is killed, which is why "it worked in background" bugs are timing-dependent.
  • Perceptible (about oom_adj 200, e.g. a foreground service or music playback) sits between visible and service in the internal numbering. The public docs collapse this into the four classes above.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Check the current class from inside the app:

val info = ActivityManager.RunningAppProcessInfo()
ActivityManager.getMyMemoryState(info)
// IMPORTANCE_FOREGROUND=100, VISIBLE=200, PERCEPTIBLE=230, SERVICE=300, CACHED=400
Log.d("Proc", "importance=${info.importance} reason=${info.importanceReasonCode}")
adb shell dumpsys activity processes | grep -A3 "ProcessRecord.*com.example"
adb shell cat /proc/$(adb shell pidof com.example)/oom_score_adj

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "background" as one bucket. Visible, service and cached behave very differently.
  • Believing a thread or a static object keeps the process alive. Only components (and their bindings) count.
  • Treating the importance constants (100/200/...) as oom_adj values. They are an API enum, not the kernel scores.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a process with a paused Activity behind a dialog foreground? → No, it is visible; the dialog-hosting Activity is on top, ours is paused but still visible.
  2. What happens to the class when the user presses Home? → Activity stops, process drops to service (if a service runs) or cached.
  3. How does a Broadcast receiver affect class? → While onReceive executes the process is treated as foreground, which is why it can be started cold even from cached.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists the four names. Senior ties them to oom_adj, explains that the process, not the Activity, is ranked, that dependencies propagate rank, and that cached processes are the unit the OS reclaims.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams chase "random" state loss in background because a cached process was killed after 20 minutes on a 3 GB device while their QA phone never reclaimed it.

questions.promptHtml: Define cold, warm and hot app start. What work happens in each, and which one do you optimise for?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Startup metrics are a standard senior signal. I want to hear "what exists already" for each case, not three memorised phrases.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Cold start means no process exists: the system forks one, creates the Application, then creates and shows the Activity. Warm start means the process is alive but the Activity must be recreated, so we skip process creation but still pay onCreate and first frame. Hot start means the Activity is in memory and the system just brings it to the front, running onRestart/onStart/onResume. I optimise cold start first because it is the worst case and what most new users and low-memory devices hit.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Cold:  tap -> fork Zygote -> bindApplication -> Application.onCreate
            -> Activity.onCreate -> first frame (TTID)
Warm:  process alive, Activity gone/recreated
            -> Activity.onCreate -> first frame        (no process or Application cost)
Hot:   process alive, Activity alive (stopped)
            -> onRestart -> onStart -> onResume -> frame
  • Cold start includes everything: process spawn, class loading with no warm caches, Application and ContentProvider init, layout inflation, first draw. Disk cache and ART code are also cold, so the same code is slower than in warm start.
  • Warm start has several variants: user backs out and reopens (Activity destroyed, process kept), or process survived onTrimMemory. State restore from savedInstanceState can matter here.
  • Hot start is the cheapest; the cost is mainly re-acquiring resources released in onStop and relayout.
  • Play Console Android vitals flags excessive start as roughly cold at 5 s or more, warm at 2 s or more, hot at 1.5 s or more. Verify current thresholds in the Play Console vitals docs.
  • Measure with adb shell am start -W -n pkg/.Main (reports ThisTime, TotalTime, WaitTime), the Displayed logcat line, and Macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric (profiling depth is A6).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Benchmarking only while the app is already in memory, which measures warm/hot and hides real user experience.
  • Believing process still alive means Application.onCreate runs again. It does not; only a new process does.
  • Calling a start "cold" after swiping the app from Recents: on many OEM builds that kills the process, on AOSP it often does not, so the next start is warm.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you force a true cold start for testing? → adb shell am force-stop pkg then launch, or Macrobenchmark StartupMode.COLD.
  2. What is TTID versus TTFD? → Time to initial display (first frame) versus time to full display, reported when you call reportFullyDrawn().
  3. Why can a warm start be slower than expected? → Heavy onCreate work plus restore of large saved state, with the process under memory pressure.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE gives three definitions. Senior states what each case skips, how to force and measure each, vitals thresholds, and that the first launch after install or low memory is cold and runs without ART profile benefit.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A release looked fine in local testing (warm) but vitals showed cold start p90 at 4.8 s on 2 GB devices because SDKs initialised in Application.onCreate.

questions.promptHtml: What is onTrimMemory, what do its levels mean, and what should an app do in response?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the only cooperative channel from the OS about memory. I want to see whether the candidate knows it is a hint, not a guarantee, and that it is not the same as being killed.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: onTrimMemory(level) is a ComponentCallbacks2 callback telling the app the system wants memory back. TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN fires when all UI becomes hidden, so drop UI-only caches like bitmaps. The RUNNING_* levels say we are still on screen while the device is low on memory. The BACKGROUND/MODERATE/COMPLETE levels say we are in the cached LRU list and how close to the kill end we are. On each I release caches I can rebuild. I never rely on it, since the process can be killed without any callback.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Level (value)                    Meaning                          Typical action
TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_MODERATE  5  we run; device getting low       trim big optional caches
TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_LOW      10  we run; device low               trim more
TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_CRITICAL 15  we run; system will start        free everything rebuildable
                                 killing background procs
TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN        20  no UI visible any more           release UI memory (bitmaps)
TRIM_MEMORY_BACKGROUND       40  now in cached list, near top     release more
TRIM_MEMORY_MODERATE         60  middle of cached list            release most
TRIM_MEMORY_COMPLETE         80  next to be killed                release all you can
  • The levels split into two groups: 5/10/15 are about foreground-ish processes, 20 is a UI signal, 40/60/80 describe your position in the cached LRU list.
  • onLowMemory() is the old equivalent of RUNNING_CRITICAL.
  • API 34 caveat: Android 14 docs mark several levels deprecated (the RUNNING_* and the BACKGROUND/MODERATE/COMPLETE ones) with the note that apps are no longer notified of them. As I recall, TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN remains the one you can rely on. Verify against the current ComponentCallbacks2 reference before stating this in an interview as fact.
  • Register in Application (or any Context.registerComponentCallbacks). Image libraries (Coil, Glide) already do this for their memory caches.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class App : Application() {
    override fun onTrimMemory(level: Int) {
        super.onTrimMemory(level)
        if (level >= ComponentCallbacks2.TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN) {
            thumbnailCache.evictAll()          // UI-only, rebuildable
        }
        if (level >= ComponentCallbacks2.TRIM_MEMORY_BACKGROUND) {
            searchIndexCache.clear()
        }
    }
}

Wrong: persisting user data in this callback. Time is short and you may be killed anyway.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Comparing with == instead of >=. Levels are ordinal pressure; handle "at least".
  • Doing I/O or heavy work in the callback; it runs on the main thread.
  • Assuming that being trimmed means being killed soon, or that no callback means safe.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is it called per Activity? → No, per process; Application or a registered callback receives it.
  2. How does this relate to LMK? → Trim is advisory and earlier; lmkd kills by oom_adj later, with no callback (Q094).
  3. How do you test it? → adb shell am send-trim-memory <pkg> MODERATE, with caveats on newer releases.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE names a couple of levels. Senior groups them, explains LRU position semantics, notes the API 34 deprecations, and says caches must be rebuildable because kill can skip the callback entirely.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An image-heavy feed had 14 percent of OOM kills in background on low-end devices until it cleared decoded bitmaps at UI_HIDDEN, which shrank the cached process footprint and made it a later kill candidate.

questions.promptHtml: How does Android decide which process to kill under memory pressure? Explain oom_adj, lmkd, and how it relates to the importance classes.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who treat "OS kills the app" as magic from those who can predict who dies first and why.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: AMS assigns every process an oom_score_adj from its components' state: roughly 0 for foreground, 100 visible, 200 perceptible, 500 service, 900 and up for cached. It pushes the value to lmkd, a native daemon. When memory pressure hits, lmkd kills the process with the highest score first, and among equals prefers the larger one. So cached, big, old processes die first, the foreground app last. The kill is SIGKILL: no callback, no onDestroy.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
oom_score_adj   Meaning (AOSP ProcessList)
-1000           native / never kill
 -900           system
 -800           persistent (e.g. phone)
    0           FOREGROUND_APP
  100           VISIBLE_APP
  200           PERCEPTIBLE_APP (FGS, music)
  300           BACKUP
  400           HEAVY_WEIGHT
  500           SERVICE (A list)
  600           HOME
  700           PREVIOUS_APP
  800           SERVICE_B
  900-999       CACHED (LRU, 900 = most recent)
  • Values are tunable per release; the ordering is what to remember. Verify numbers against ProcessList.java for your target release.
  • Evolution: the kernel lowmemorykiller driver was replaced by userspace lmkd (Android 9+; kernel driver removed in later kernels). Classic lmkd used minfree thresholds: when free memory falls under the level paired with an adj, kill processes at or above that adj. Newer devices use PSI (Pressure Stall Information): kill when time stalled on memory exceeds a threshold, not just when free pages are low.
  • Legacy threshold example: minfree 18432 pages x 4096 B/page = 75,497,472 B = 72 MiB free paired with adj 0, so when free memory drops below 72 MiB, even foreground-level processes become candidates. The numbers are illustrative and vary by device RAM class.
  • Selection: highest adj, then largest RSS/PSS inside that band. A bloated cached process dies before a small one.
  • AMS also trims cached count (a cap on the cached/empty list, device-specific) so processes are killed even without pressure.
  • Kill differences: lmkd kills (SIGKILL), AMS trims, and Process.killProcess/crashes are the app's own. All of them end in the same state for the user: Application re-created on next start.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
adb shell dumpsys activity processes | grep -E "ProcessRecord|oom:"
adb shell cat /proc/<pid>/oom_score_adj
adb shell logcat -b events | grep -i lmk          # kill events on many builds
adb shell dumpsys meminfo -a | head -80            # summary by oom class

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking foreground apps can never be killed. Under severe pressure lmkd kills them too.
  • Saying the app's onTrimMemory guards you. Trim is advice, lmkd is enforcement.
  • Mixing up oom_adj (old scale, -17..15) with oom_score_adj (-1000..1000).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Who sets the value? → ActivityManagerService computes it from component state and sends it to lmkd over a socket.
  2. Why did a small app die before a huge one? → Different adj bands; band beats size.
  3. How does PSI differ from minfree? → PSI reacts to actual stall time instead of free page counts, so it handles file cache and fragmentation better.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "least recently used apps die". Senior gives the adj ladder, names AMS and lmkd, notes band-then-size selection and the PSI shift, and shows tools to verify.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A low-end device cohort showed early deaths because the app's PSS in cached state was 3x competitors, so it was always the biggest cached kill.

questions.promptHtml: What actually keeps an Android process alive in the background, and what does not?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates think a thread, a WakeLock or START_STICKY keeps them alive. I want the exact distinction.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The system keeps a process ranked by its components, not by what its threads are doing. A resumed Activity, a foreground service, a running receiver, a service bound by an important client or a provider in use make the process important. A bare Thread, a Handler, a static object, a WakeLock or a notification does not. START_STICKY does not keep the process alive; it asks the system to restart the service after the process is killed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Raises importance               Does NOT raise importance
-----------------------------   -----------------------------------
Activity resumed / visible      Running Thread / Executor
Foreground service              Coroutine in a CoroutineScope
BroadcastReceiver in onReceive  Static fields, singletons
Service bound by important      PowerManager WakeLock (CPU awake only)
  client (Q104)                 Posted notification (unless FGS)
Provider with active client     START_STICKY by itself
Running JobScheduler job        Alarm scheduled for later
Instrumentation / persistent    "I'm doing network IO"
  • A started, non-foreground service gets the service class (oom 500), which is killable and, on Android 8+, stopped after the app has been in background for about a minute (background execution limits, see chunk 08/17).
  • A running JobScheduler/WorkManager job is a component that keeps the process ranked while the job runs, but with a finite execution window.
  • WakeLock keeps the CPU from sleeping; it does not change the process rank, so lmkd can still kill you holding it.
  • Receivers are tightly bounded: foreground broadcast about 10 s, background about 60 s on older rules; goAsync extends but is also bounded (chunk 09).
  • For work that must survive, you need a component with the right type (foreground service with a declared type, expedited work) or a design that survives death (resumable, persisted queue).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Looks safe, is not: thread has no component backing it.
class Uploader {
    fun start(file: File) = Thread { upload(file) }.start() // dies with the process
}
// Better: persisted, resumable work
WorkManager.getInstance(ctx).enqueueUniqueWork(
    "upload-${file.name}", ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP,
    OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<UploadWorker>()
        .setConstraints(Constraints(requiredNetworkType = NetworkType.CONNECTED))
        .build()
)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a WakeLock as a "keep alive" mechanism and burning battery with no priority gain.
  • Confusing "restarts after death" with "does not die".
  • Assuming a foreground service never dies: it ranks high but is still killable under extreme pressure and has type timeouts on Android 15 (chunk 08).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. START_STICKY vs START_REDELIVER_INTENT? → Both restart the service after kill; the second redelivers the last Intent, the first delivers null.
  2. Does a coroutine in viewModelScope survive Home? → Only as long as the process survives; no protection.
  3. Does JobScheduler guarantee completion? → No; it guarantees an opportunity within constraints, and the job can be stopped and retried.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "use a service". Senior says components set rank, lists non-keepalive illusions, and designs for death with persisted, resumable work.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A sync used a plain executor after a SyncAdapter removal; 6 percent of syncs silently ended partway when users pressed Home on 3 GB devices.

questions.promptHtml: When exactly does Application.onCreate run relative to other components, how often, and what are the consequences for what you put there?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Application.onCreate is the usual cause of slow starts and wrong-process init. I want to see the ordering, the per-process rule, and a discipline for what goes in it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Application.onCreate runs once per process, on the main thread, before any Activity, Service, or Receiver is created in that process. Declared ContentProviders in that process are installed before it runs, so provider-based SDK init fires even earlier. It does not run again on rotation or Activity recreation, but it does run on every cold start, including starts triggered by a broadcast or JobScheduler with no UI. So it should be tiny: no I/O, no heavy SDKs, nothing that assumes a UI.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Zygote fork
  -> ActivityThread.main -> attach -> AMS.attachApplication
  -> handleBindApplication
       1. create Application, attachBaseContext(base)   <- Application ctor / attachBaseContext
       2. installContentProviders(...)                  <- provider.onCreate  (initOrder)
       3. Application.onCreate()                        <- yours
  -> then the component that triggered the start:
       Activity.onCreate / Service.onCreate / Receiver.onReceive
  • Because providers run before onCreate, libraries using InitializationProvider (Jetpack App Startup) or old Firebase auto-init run before your Application code. Heavy init hidden there still counts toward cold start.
  • Every process start runs it, including a silent start from an alarm or an FCM push. A 400 ms onCreate multiplies across background wakeups (battery) and delays the receiver (it executes after onCreate).
  • On the main thread, onCreate blocks first frame: it sits in the cold-start critical path.
  • It is not the place to persist anything or to rely on being called when state is lost: after process death the next start calls it again and your singletons are empty (chunk 04).
  • Multi-process: runs once per process (Q098).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class App : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        // Cheap and mandatory only: crash reporting, StrictMode in debug, DI graph shell
        if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) StrictMode.enableDefaults()
        // Defer the rest
        ProcessLifecycleOwner.get().lifecycle.addObserver(LazyInit)   // after first UI
    }
}
object LazyInit : DefaultLifecycleObserver {
    override fun onStart(owner: LifecycleOwner) {
        owner.lifecycle.removeObserver(this)
        // analytics, remote config prefetch on a background thread
    }
}

Broken: Database.build(...).allowMainThreadQueries() or Firebase.remoteConfig.fetchAndActivate().await() in onCreate.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Initialising everything "just in case" in onCreate, then being surprised that a push notification wake costs 600 ms.
  • Assuming a UI exists or that Context is an Activity.
  • Using Application.onCreate as proof that the app was launched by the user.
  • Forgetting attachBaseContext runs earlier (used for multidex/locale wrapping).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not run everything on a background thread? → It is fine for non-UI init, but then you own ordering and races; a thread started there can still be needed by the first Activity.
  2. Where do ContentProviders fit? → Before onCreate, ordered by android:initOrder, only for providers hosted in this process.
  3. How would you audit it? → Perfetto/Trace.beginSection markers around each init, or App Startup dependency graph; measure with Macrobenchmark.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "initialise libraries there". Senior gives the full ordering including providers, that it runs per process and per background wake, and treats it as a critical-path budget.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A push-heavy app discovered 30 percent of cold starts were headless (broadcast wakes) and every one paid for an ad SDK init that only the UI needed.

questions.contextHtml:
A video-sharing app uploads 80 MB clips. The upload runs in a coroutine launched from viewModelScope through a plain UploadRepository. DAU is 600k; about 9 percent of uploads never finish. Failures cluster on 3 GB devices when the user presses Home or switches to the camera. QA on a Pixel 8 cannot reproduce. Logcat from a failing user (via bug report):

ActivityManager: Killing 14873:com.example.clips/u0a312 (adj 920): empty #17
lmkd: Kill 'com.example.clips' (14873), uid 10312, oom_score_adj 920 to free 212MB rss

The backend shows a partial multipart upload that is never completed. The server team blames mobile network flakiness.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening, how do you confirm it, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Network issue, add retries" or "use a bigger thread pool / WakeLock". It never asks why the upload stopped, so retries run in a process that no longer exists. Another weak answer: "make the service START_STICKY", which restarts with a null Intent and no work state.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How long after Home do uploads die (seconds vs minutes)? Which devices and Android versions? Is the upload tied to a visible UI or a service? Is there a server-side session so we can resume? Why: the timing separates lmkd from Doze or app bugs.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Show a persistent "uploading" notification only if already a foreground service; otherwise ship a hotfix that enqueues uploads as expedited work and warns the user not to leave on the first-run flow. Server: expire stale partial uploads so users can retry cleanly.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The process was killed by lmkd after dropping to cached; evidence is adj 920 ... empty. (b) Doze/standby throttling (less likely, device is active). (c) App crash. (d) Server timeout. Red herring: the "flaky network" claim.
  4. How I'd verify each: Read ApplicationExitInfo on next launch (REASON_LOW_MEMORY, importance CACHED, Q103). Reproduce with adb shell am kill com.example.clips after pressing Home (kills background process like the OS). Check adb logcat -b events | grep lmk. Crashlytics for no crash at that time.
  5. Root cause: Work was owned by viewModelScope, which lives only in the process. After Home the Activity stops, no component remains, rank falls to cached (oom ~900+), and lmkd kills it under pressure. Nothing persisted the upload state.
  6. Fix: Short-term: move to WorkManager with setExpedited and a foreground notification (an FGS type of dataSync on Android 14, with Android 15 timeout limits; see chunk 08). Long-term: resumable, chunked uploads (for example 4 MB chunks) with the offset stored in Room, so a restart continues instead of restarting 80 MB.
class UploadWorker(ctx: Context, p: WorkerParameters) : CoroutineWorker(ctx, p) {
    override suspend fun doWork(): Result {
        val offset = dao.offset(id)           // persisted resume point
        return if (uploadFrom(offset)) Result.success() else Result.retry()
    }
    override suspend fun getForegroundInfo() = ForegroundInfo(
        NOTIF_ID, buildNotification(),
        ServiceInfo.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_TYPE_DATA_SYNC
    )
}
  1. Prevention: Chaos test that kills the process mid-upload in CI (am kill), an alert on upload completion ratio by RAM class, and a code review rule that user-visible long work never lives only in a ViewModel or Thread.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use a permanent foreground service for all uploads (battery, policy). I would not rely on START_STICKY, a WakeLock, or ignore battery optimisation prompts as the primary fix.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The user force-stops the app. → Work is cancelled; WorkManager reschedules only after the next app launch. Say it honestly.
  • Android 15 limits dataSync FGS to about 6 hours per 24 hours. → Chunk and resume; use expedited work with a fallback to regular constrained work (verify the current limit in the FGS timeouts doc).
  • Uploads must continue while offline then resume. → Constraint CONNECTED plus persisted state; the Worker re-enqueues itself.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A media app lost 11 percent of uploads on low-end devices for months, blamed on carriers. A REASON_LOW_MEMORY histogram from exit info showed the pattern in one afternoon; resumable chunks fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds retries/WakeLock, does not recognise process death.
  • Hire: Identifies cached-process kill, moves to WorkManager/FGS.
  • Strong hire: Proves it with exit info and am kill, adds resumable chunking and a kill-in-CI test, and knows FGS type/timeout constraints.

questions.promptHtml: What does android:process do? What changes for your app when components run in a second process?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Multi-process is easy to turn on and a common source of bugs. A senior should list what is no longer shared and why people do it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: android:process runs a component in a different OS process. A name starting with a colon, like :remote, is private to the app; a lowercase dotted name is global and shareable between apps with the same UID. Each process gets its own VM, heap budget, static state, and its own Application instance whose onCreate runs separately. So singletons, caches, and in-memory flags are not shared; you need IPC (Binder, ContentProvider, files, a Room multi-instance setup) to communicate. People use it for crash isolation, memory isolation, or an independent lifecycle like a player or push process.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
UID 10123 (one app)
 +-- pid 4100  com.example          Application #1, heap, statics
 +-- pid 4188  com.example:remote   Application #2, heap, statics   (separate)
        shared: APK, files on disk, same UID permissions
        NOT shared: memory, singletons, SharedPreferences cache, DB connection cache
  • Each process pays the base runtime cost (loading framework, ART, your classes). Treat tens of MB of PSS as the typical order of magnitude and measure with dumpsys meminfo.
  • Application.onCreate runs in every process. Code must branch on process name (Q099).
  • ContentProviders are instantiated only in the process they declare (android:process, default: main process). Auto-init providers (Firebase, App Startup) therefore do not run in :remote, so libraries may be uninitialised there.
  • SharedPreferences is not multi-process safe (MODE_MULTI_PROCESS is deprecated and unreliable). Use a ContentProvider, DataStore with a single process owner (the multi-process DataStore variant exists but check its guide), or Binder.
  • Room: use enableMultiInstanceInvalidation() so observers in process A see writes from B.
  • WebView: since API 28 a second process must set a distinct data directory suffix (Q101).
  • Lifecycle: processes are ranked and killed independently. The UI process may die while :remote lives, or vice versa.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<service android:name=".SyncService" android:process=":sync" android:exported="false"/>
<service android:name=".ShareService" android:process="com.example.shared"/>
fun Context.isMainProcess() = Application.getProcessName() == packageName   // API 28+

For API < 28 read /proc/self/cmdline or compare against ActivityManager.runningAppProcesses.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming a singleton Config is shared: it is initialised twice with possibly different values.
  • Using MODE_MULTI_PROCESS or file-locking as a hand-rolled sync mechanism.
  • Putting android:process on a component only to escape a memory problem, without measuring the extra baseline.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a component in :remote share the Application subclass? → Same class, a different instance and onCreate call.
  2. When is a global (non-colon) process name valid? → When apps share a UID/signature; not common in modern apps.
  3. How do you share a hot object cheaply? → You cannot; pass IDs/URIs/ParcelFileDescriptor/shared memory, not object graphs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "runs in another process". Senior lists exactly what stops being shared, the cost per process, per-process Application and providers, and designs process-name-aware init.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A chat team split the push receiver into :push and found cold start metrics doubled because both processes ran full init (Q099).

questions.contextHtml:
A fintech app has a bound SyncService declared with android:process=":remote". After a release adding a periodic sync, dashboards show app_open analytics events doubled for 38 percent of sessions (about 210k extra events/day), and Crashlytics shows SQLiteDatabaseLockedException: database is locked at startup in 0.7 percent of sessions. Two log lines appear per start:

I/App: Application.onCreate pid=5120 process=com.example.fin
I/App: Application.onCreate pid=5188 process=com.example.fin:remote
W/Firebase: FirebaseApp is not initialized in this process com.example.fin:remote
class App : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        Analytics.init(this); Analytics.track("app_open")
        Db.migrateIfNeeded(this)          // runs Room migrations eagerly
        FirebaseMessaging.getInstance().token   // used by SyncService too
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Why is this happening and how do you fix it without breaking the sync?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Debounce the event on the backend" or "make Analytics a singleton". Singletons are per process, so that does not help. It also ignores the DB lock and the Firebase warning.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the second Application.onCreate line appear on every start? Does anything in :remote need analytics or the DB? Is :remote really needed (why separate process)? Why: decides between guarding init and removing the process.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix: guard onCreate with the process name so :remote skips analytics and migration. Server: dedupe events by session_id while fixing.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Each process runs Application.onCreate, so init runs twice. (b) Two processes opening the same Room DB and one running migrations eagerly causes locks. (c) Firebase auto-init provider only runs in the main process, so token calls in :remote fail. Red herring: the analytics SDK being buggy.
  4. How I'd verify each: adb shell ps -A | grep com.example.fin shows two pids. adb logcat --pid for each. Add Application.getProcessName() to every init log. Reproduce by starting the service via adb shell am startservice.
  5. Root cause: Android instantiates the Application once per process. :remote is a full process with its own Application, so global init code runs twice, while providers declared in the main process do not run in :remote.
  6. Fix: Guard by process, and make the service cheap.
class App : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        when (Application.getProcessName()) {          // API 28+
            packageName -> initMain()                  // analytics, migration, messaging
            "$packageName:remote" -> initRemote()      // minimal, only what sync needs
        }
    }
}

Long term: ask whether :remote is needed; if not, remove android:process and the problem disappears. 7. Prevention: Unit test for process-name routing, a lint/code-review checklist item "Application.onCreate is per process", and a startup log of process name in debug builds. Add enableMultiInstanceInvalidation() if two processes legitimately use Room. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use a static boolean or file lock to "initialise once"; I would not run migrations from a process that does not own the DB.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Min SDK is 26, so no getProcessName. → Read /proc/self/cmdline once and cache, or use ActivityManager.runningAppProcesses matching Process.myPid().
  • The service genuinely needs Firebase. → Initialise FirebaseApp.initializeApp(context) explicitly in initRemote().
  • Can a provider help? → Providers run in the process they declare; declare a stub provider in :remote only if you need provider-based init there (rarely worth it).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team's "installs doubled" alert was actually every cold start counted twice because a share-extension process shared Application. A single process-name guard fixed the metric and cut a startup crash.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames the SDK or dedupes server-side only.
  • Hire: Explains per-process Application and adds a process-name guard.
  • Strong hire: Also covers providers not running in :remote, DB locking, API-level fallback for the process name, and questions the need for the extra process.

questions.promptHtml: What are app standby buckets, and how do they relate to process priority? Do they change oom_adj?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: People confuse "background kill" with "background throttling". They are separate mechanisms that produce similar symptoms.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Standby buckets (API 28+) classify apps by how recently and how often the user engages with them: Active, Working set, Frequent, Rare, and later Restricted (API 30). The bucket does not change process rank or kill order. It limits what the app can do in the background: when jobs run, how many alarms fire, how many high-priority FCM messages count. So a "dead" background app may be alive but deferred, which is a different bug than lmkd.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Bucket      Meaning                                  Effect on background work (approx; verify docs)
Active      in use now / just used                   no extra limits
Working set used regularly                           jobs deferred up to ~2 h, alarms ~6/h
Frequent    used often, not daily                    jobs ~8 h, alarms ~2/h, high-priority FCM ~10/day
Rare        seldom used                              jobs ~24 h, alarms ~1/h, network deferred, FCM ~5/day
Restricted  heavy resource use or user-restricted    jobs short session ~1/day, very few alarms
Never       installed, never launched                no background work until launched
  • Rank (oom_adj) is determined by running components; buckets limit starting work. A process in the Rare bucket that is currently showing UI is still foreground.
  • Promotion: opening the app, interacting with a notification, or running an FGS moves you toward Active. The system and OEMs add heuristics.
  • Use UsageStatsManager.getAppStandbyBucket() to read your own bucket.
  • Deep treatment of Doze, alarms, FCM quotas belongs to chunk 17; here the point is separation of concerns.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
adb shell am get-standby-bucket com.example
adb shell am set-standby-bucket com.example rare
adb shell dumpsys usagestats | grep -A2 com.example
val bucket = (getSystemService(UsageStatsManager::class.java)).appStandbyBucket
Log.d("Standby", "bucket=$bucket")   // STANDBY_BUCKET_ACTIVE=10, WORKING_SET=20, FREQUENT=30, RARE=40, RESTRICTED=45

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Debugging a missed background sync as a "kill" without checking the bucket.
  • Testing only on a freshly installed device where the app is Active.
  • Quoting exact limits from memory; they vary by release and OEM.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a foreground service bypass buckets? → It lets you run work while it is running, and its use affects bucket placement; consult the docs per version.
  2. How do you test Rare bucket behavior? → am set-standby-bucket then schedule a job.
  3. Is Restricted an automatic bucket? → The system may place there for heavy usage; the user can also restrict battery in settings (varies by version).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists the bucket names. Senior separates throttling from killing, states rank is unaffected, and knows how to test it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A reminders app that users opened monthly saw 24 h delays in jobs; the Rare bucket, not lmkd, explained it.

questions.contextHtml:
A support-chat feature runs in android:process=":chat" to isolate a heavy third-party SDK. After release, Crashlytics shows a new crash at 0.4 percent of sessions, only on Android 9+ and only after opening the "Help" screen, which uses a WebView inside :chat.

java.lang.RuntimeException: Using WebView from more than one process at once
with the same data directory is not supported. https://crbug.com/558377
    at android.webkit.WebViewFactory.createProviderImpl(...)
    at android.webkit.WebView.<init>(WebView.java:...)
    at com.example.chat.HelpActivity.onCreate(HelpActivity.kt:31)
class App : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        WebView(this).settings.javaScriptEnabled = true   // warm up WebView
    }
}

The main process also uses a WebView for terms and conditions. QA only tested chat on its own.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug and explain the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Catch the exception" or "move WebView to a background thread". It does not see that the cause is two processes sharing one on-disk WebView data directory.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which processes create WebViews? Min SDK? Is the warm-up in onCreate executed in both processes? Why: Application.onCreate runs in :chat too (Q099).
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix to guard the warm-up and set the suffix; disable the Help WebView in :chat via remote flag if the fix is delayed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Two processes created WebView with the same data directory (the message says so). (b) Thread misuse (CalledFromWrongThreadException would be a different error). (c) WebView provider update mismatch.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce on API 28+ by opening the main-process WebView and then Help; adb shell ps shows two pids. Inspect /data/data/pkg/app_webview* directories.
  5. Root cause: Since API 28 Android enforces one process per WebView data directory because Chromium locks it. The warm-up in Application.onCreate runs in every process, and :chat ends up using the same directory the main process uses.
  6. Fix: Call WebView.setDataDirectorySuffix() before any WebView use in the second process, once per process.
class App : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        val name = Application.getProcessName()                       // API 28+
        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 28 && name != packageName) {
            WebView.setDataDirectorySuffix(name.substringAfter(':'))  // e.g. "chat"
        }
    }
}

Do the warm-up only in the process that needs it. The suffix must be set before the first WebView or CookieManager call. 7. Prevention: Instrumented test that launches each process entry point; lint/checklist for android:process that lists WebView, DB, prefs. Remember cookies and storage are separate per suffix: login state in the main WebView is not visible in :chat. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not catch the exception (it hides the problem). I would not ignore session continuity: with different suffixes, logins do not share; pass tokens explicitly. I would reconsider why the SDK needs its own process.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Min SDK 24. → The enforcement is API 28+, but sharing a directory is still unsafe; use the same guard where available and avoid multi-process WebView below it.
  • CookieManager already used before the suffix? → The suffix call throws IllegalStateException; order of init matters.
  • Does a second process double memory? → Yes, includes a second WebView renderer setup; weigh the cost.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A launch slipped by a week because QA never opened WebView after the chat process; the first crash report named the right file but the warm-up line lived in Application.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Catches the exception or threads.
  • Hire: Identifies the shared data directory and uses setDataDirectorySuffix.
  • Strong hire: Also spots the Application.onCreate warm-up running per process, discusses cookie isolation, init order, and challenges the need for a separate process.

questions.subtopic: Deaths that are not low-memory kills
questions.promptHtml: Besides low-memory kills, what can end your app's process while the user is using it or just after, and how does each differ in what you can observe or handle?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior engineers triage "the app restarted" by cause. I want a taxonomy, not "it crashed".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: There are several. An uncaught exception or native signal kills our own process. An ANR makes the system kill it (or the user taps Close). Revoking a runtime permission in Settings kills the process. Updating or reinstalling the app kills it. Force-stop kills it and also blocks background components until next launch. A dependency dying (a provider we are a client of) can kill us. Under heavy pressure lmkd can even kill the foreground app. OEM battery managers add their own kills. Each leaves different evidence, and only some give a callback.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Cause                          Callback to app?          Evidence / API
Uncaught Java exception        UncaughtExceptionHandler  crash reporter, EXIT_INFO REASON_CRASH
Native crash (SIGSEGV)         none (signal)             tombstone, REASON_CRASH_NATIVE
ANR                            none                      traces, REASON_ANR
lmkd / low memory              none (SIGKILL)            REASON_LOW_MEMORY
Excessive resource usage       none                      REASON_EXCESSIVE_RESOURCE_USAGE
Permission revoked in Settings none                      REASON_PERMISSION_CHANGE
User force-stop / removal      none                      REASON_USER_REQUESTED (and records cleared on stop on some versions)
Update / reinstall             none                      REASON_OTHER
Dependency died (provider)     none                      REASON_DEPENDENCY_DIED
  • Permission revocation and updates are deliberate kills; the next launch reads fresh state, which is why permission checks must run every time, not once (chunk 15).
  • Force-stop sets the package "stopped": alarms, jobs and broadcasts are cleared until the user opens the app again.
  • Swiping the app out of Recents: AOSP removes the task but usually leaves the process cached; many OEM builds kill it. Behaviour is not portable.
  • Memory pressure can kill the foreground app (adj 0) when lmkd is out of lower-priority victims.
  • None of the kills run onDestroy; do not store critical data there. Persist eagerly.
  • Observability: ApplicationExitInfo (API 30+) gives a reason per death (Q103); Crashlytics only sees crashes and ANRs.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
adb shell am kill com.example             # kills cached (background) process like the OS
adb shell am force-stop com.example       # also marks stopped
adb shell pm revoke com.example android.permission.CAMERA   # kills the app
adb shell kill -9 <pid>                   # SIGKILL, simulates lmkd

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating every unexpected restart as a crash bug.
  • Using am force-stop to test process death: it clears scheduled work, giving a worse environment than a real kill. Use am kill.
  • Relying on onDestroy or onTerminate (never called on devices) for cleanup.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does revoking a permission kill the app? → Granted state is fixed at process level for mapped resources; killing guarantees no code runs with stale access.
  2. Can you intercept SIGKILL? → No. Only a persisted design survives it.
  3. What is REASON_DEPENDENCY_DIED? → We were bound to or using something whose process died, such as a provider client; the system may take us down.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE blames memory or crashes. Senior classifies by cause, knows what is observable for each, and tests with the correct simulation command.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A support team's "random logouts" were permission revocations killing the process while the in-memory token cache was never restored.

questions.promptHtml: How can an app find out why its previous process died? Walk me through ApplicationExitInfo and how you would use it in production.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Crash reporters only see crashes. A senior knows there is a platform API for kills and uses it to separate lmkd, ANR, and user actions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Since API 30, ActivityManager.getHistoricalProcessExitReasons() returns recent exit records for my package: reason (low memory, ANR, crash, user requested, permission change...), the importance at death, PSS/RSS, a description, a timestamp, and for ANRs a trace stream. I read it on next launch and send a compact event to analytics. I can also attach my own state with setProcessStateSummary() and get it back in the record, so I know what the user was doing when the process died.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Records are kept by the system in a small, bounded history per package. I recall about 16 entries, but treat the exact size as not guaranteed. They are lost on uninstall and not available below API 30.
  • Fields that matter: reason, importance (the rank at the time, which separates "killed while cached" from "killed while foreground"), pss/rss (memory size when it died), status (signal or exit code), description (system text), processStateSummary (bytes I set), and traceInputStream (ANR or native crash trace in some cases).
  • Interpretation:
    • REASON_LOW_MEMORY with IMPORTANCE_CACHED: ordinary lmkd reclaim; fine unless it breaks work.
    • REASON_LOW_MEMORY with IMPORTANCE_FOREGROUND: our footprint is hurting; investigate memory (chunk 12).
    • REASON_ANR: look at the trace (A6).
    • REASON_USER_REQUESTED: user action (swipe or force-stop depending on OEM).
    • REASON_PERMISSION_CHANGE, REASON_EXCESSIVE_RESOURCE_USAGE, REASON_DEPENDENCY_DIED.
  • It does not tell you why the memory was needed. Combine with your own breadcrumbs.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@RequiresApi(30)
fun logLastExits(ctx: Context) {
    val am = ctx.getSystemService(ActivityManager::class.java)
    am.getHistoricalProcessExitReasons(ctx.packageName, 0, 5).forEach { e ->
        analytics.track(
            "proc_exit",
            "reason" to e.reason, "importance" to e.importance,
            "rss_mb" to e.rss / 1024,                       // rss is in KB
            "desc" to e.description,
            "state" to e.processStateSummary?.decodeToString()
        )
    }
}
// While running, record the screen/flow so it is returned after death
ActivityManager::class.java.let {
    ctx.getSystemService(it).setProcessStateSummary("upload-flow".encodeToByteArray())
}

Use pid of the record to deduplicate across launches; do not log the same exit every time.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling it every launch and counting the same record repeatedly.
  • Assuming the list contains every death; it is bounded and API 30+.
  • Using it to "recover" state. It is diagnostics; recovery is chunk 04 territory.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does it differ from a crash reporter? → It sees kills and ANRs with no in-process handler, but offers no stack except limited traces.
  2. Can you use it for ANR traces? → Yes, traceInputStream for ANR records; large payloads, so sample.
  3. How would you dashboard it? → Exit reason by importance and RAM class and app version, alerting when LOW_MEMORY at FOREGROUND rises.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE cites Crashlytics. Senior uses exit info for kill taxonomy, ties importance to the cause, and adds a state summary.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team found 70 percent of "lost session" tickets were cached-importance low-memory kills, which redirected effort from crash fixing to state persistence.

questions.promptHtml: A service in a separate process is bound by your Activity. How does that affect each process's priority, and which flags change the behavior?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand that process rank is a dependency graph and can predict who survives and who is taken down together.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A bound service process is ranked at least as high as its most important client, as long as the binding is a normal one. If my UI process is foreground, the service process is lifted to match. If my UI goes to cached, the service falls with it unless something else holds it. Content providers work the same way: a process hosting a provider with an active client is ranked with that client. Flags such as BIND_WAIVE_PRIORITY, BIND_NOT_FOREGROUND, BIND_ABOVE_CLIENT, and BIND_IMPORTANT adjust this.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
UI process (foreground, adj 0)
   |  bindService(BIND_AUTO_CREATE)
   v
:player process  -> raised to ~0 while the UI is foreground
UI to background (cached, adj 900+)
:player process  -> no longer raised; drops toward service/cached ranking
  • AMS computes adj per process, then raises it to the best of its clients' adj (with caps depending on flags). There is no raising if the client itself is cached.
  • Provider links work similarly: the process hosting a provider is as important as its most important client.
  • Flags (all Context.BIND_*):
    • BIND_AUTO_CREATE: create the service if needed (does not affect rank by itself).
    • BIND_WAIVE_PRIORITY: client's importance is not propagated; service ranks on its own.
    • BIND_NOT_FOREGROUND: do not lift above the background class.
    • BIND_ABOVE_CLIENT: service is ranked above the client (used by system components that must outlive their client).
    • BIND_IMPORTANT: treats the binding as foreground-important for the service.
  • Practical result: a music player that binds only from a UI dies when the UI dies. A started foreground service keeps its own rank independent of clients.
  • Death coupling: if the service process dies, the client gets onServiceDisconnected; if the client dies, the service is unbound and may stop. Binder death callbacks are chunk 14.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Service rank follows UI: music stops when UI goes to cached
bindService(intent, conn, Context.BIND_AUTO_CREATE)

// Service keeps its own life: start as foreground, bind as client
ContextCompat.startForegroundService(this, intent)
bindService(intent, conn, Context.BIND_AUTO_CREATE or Context.BIND_WAIVE_PRIORITY)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming a bound service has its own priority independent of the client.
  • Forgetting provider clients: a heavy :db process can be held at high priority by a background reader.
  • Using BIND_IMPORTANT to avoid a design change. It increases pressure on the system.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does binding from a Service client help? → Only as much as that service's rank.
  2. How can you see the dependency chain? → adb shell dumpsys activity processes lists connections and reasons ("adj reason").
  3. What does startForeground do for a bound service? → Gives it its own foreground-service rank regardless of clients.
