sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says bound services live while bound. Senior explains rank inheritance, caps, flags, provider links and how to read it in dumpsys.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A navigation app's routing process died every time the user locked the phone, because the UI-only bind lost priority once the UI cached.

questions.contextHtml:
A marketplace app with 800k DAU shipped version 7.4. Android vitals: cold start p90 rose from 1.9 s to 3.1 s; on 2 GB devices (40 percent of the base) p90 is 4.6 s and 1-star reviews mention "slow open". The diff added six SDKs: analytics, attribution, crash, remote config, ads, and a feature-flag SDK, all initialised in Application.onCreate plus two via App Startup providers. Logcat:

I/ActivityTaskManager: Displayed com.example/.MainActivity: +3s112ms
I/Choreographer: Skipped 74 frames! The application may be doing too much work on its main thread.

Product wants all SDKs ready before the first screen "for correct attribution". Push-notification wakes (40 percent of process starts) also got slower.
questions.promptHtml: How do you diagnose the regression and decide what to initialise when?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Move everything to a background thread" without checking dependencies, or "remove SDKs". It ignores which inits are on the critical path and the cost of headless process starts.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which SDKs truly must run before the first frame (usually crash reporting only)? Does attribution tolerate a few seconds of delay? What share of process starts are headless? What is the budget (for example p90 under 2.2 s on 2 GB)? Why: sets a defensible startup contract with product.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Feature-flag or defer the two worst SDKs in a hotfix (ads and attribution can start after first draw); ship a Baseline Profile if not present (profile tooling is A6).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Serial SDK init on the main thread in onCreate and providers. (b) Class loading/dex cost with no ART profile on first runs. (c) Disk or prefs I/O on main. (d) Layout inflation in the first screen. Red herring: network latency, since nothing waits on the network.
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto trace of a cold start with custom Trace.beginSection("init:ads") markers; adb shell am start -W; Macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric on a mid/low-end device; simpleperf for hot methods; StrictMode for disk reads.
  5. Root cause: About 1.2 s of serial main-thread SDK init (for instance 5 SDKs averaging 240 ms: 5 x 240 = 1,200 ms) in the process-start critical path, paid even by headless starts.
  6. Fix: Short-term: split init into tiers.
class App : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        Crash.init(this)                         // tier 0: must be first
        appScope.launch(Dispatchers.Default) {   // tier 1: not UI-blocking
            Flags.init(this@App); Analytics.init(this@App)
        }
        ProcessLifecycleOwner.get().lifecycle.addObserver(Tier2Init) // tier 2: after UI
    }
}

Long-term: App Startup with explicit dependencies, tools:node="remove" on providers that auto-init, and skip UI-only SDKs in headless starts (check ProcessLifecycleOwner state or a launch intent flag). 7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark in CI with a startup budget gate, a registry that forces each SDK to declare its tier, and review of manifest merge output for new providers. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make everything lazy-on-first-use without owners (surprise stalls later). I would not push attribution to never; I would negotiate a tolerance window. I would not hide cost by showing a longer splash.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Background init now races with the first screen needing a flag. → Provide default values and a ready signal; the screen renders with defaults and updates.
  • Android 12 splash API hides the delay. → It hides the white flash, not the TTID; measure real time.
  • Ad SDK refuses lazy init. → Isolate it behind an adapter and measure its cost; escalate with data or swap vendor.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shopping app recovered 900 ms at p90 by moving three SDKs off the critical path and gating one behind first scroll; the "attribution loss" feared by marketing measured at 0.3 percent.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "Use a background thread" without measurement.
  • Hire: Uses Perfetto/markers, tiers initialisation, defers non-critical SDKs.
  • Strong hire: Handles headless starts, providers, budget gates in CI, and negotiates with product using data.

questions.subtopic: Cached app freezer and phantom process limit
questions.promptHtml: What are the cached app freezer and the Android 12 phantom process killer, and how can they change behavior of an app that "worked" in the background?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Recent platform behavior that produces "app is alive but frozen" and "native child killed" bugs. Shows whether the candidate follows platform changes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The freezer, introduced in Android 11 as an optional feature and used on newer devices, freezes cached processes using the cgroup freezer, so their threads get no CPU while cached; they are not killed, just paused. Android 12 added a limit on phantom processes (native child processes forked outside the normal app components); beyond a device-wide cap (32 in AOSP, as I recall), the system kills the extras with SIGKILL. Both break code that assumed a cached process keeps running or that native children are free.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Freezer: the ActivityManager freezes a process after it has been cached for a short time (on the order of 10 s, configurable via device config) and thaws it when it is promoted (user returns, broadcast delivered, binder call). A frozen process cannot run timers, threads, or coroutines.
  • Binder interaction: synchronous binder calls into a frozen process are rejected, and the system kills a frozen process that receives certain transactions it cannot handle. Asynchronous (oneway) transactions are queued until thaw, with limits (see chunk 14).
  • What this breaks: ad hoc background threads in a cached app, in-process timers, a socket keepalive that was never legitimate.
  • Phantom processes: processes started from native code (fork/exec) rather than via Android components. Android 12 tracks them, caps the total (32 by default), and kills the oldest or those of apps in cached state. Visible symptoms: a native helper dies with signal 9 and logs mention phantom process.
  • Both features are device-config driven and vary by OEM. Verify with adb shell dumpsys activity processes and current developer docs before stating defaults.
  • Developer escape hatches exist (a developer option for child process restrictions on Android 12L and later; device config for the cap) but they are for debugging, not for shipping.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# Developer-only: see freezer state in the process dump
adb shell dumpsys activity processes | grep -i frozen
# Android 12/12L debug workaround for phantom cap (not for production; verify on your build)
adb shell device_config put activity_manager max_phantom_processes 2147483647
// Wrong: expects a native worker to run indefinitely from a non-component context.
ProcessBuilder("ffmpeg", "-i", src).start()
// Right: own it from a component with a legitimate lifetime (foreground service / bound service),
// keep the work resumable, and handle a SIGKILL exit code.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Debugging a frozen process as a deadlock: it is correct behavior.
  • Spawning long-lived native subprocesses and trusting they survive.
  • Using the dev workaround as a product fix.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a frozen process still hold memory? → Yes; it remains a kill candidate for lmkd.
  2. How does a push message reach a frozen app? → The system thaws it to deliver the broadcast or binder call.
  3. How do you detect your child was killed? → Exit status 137 (128 plus 9) from Process.waitFor().

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE has not heard of either. Senior knows the symptoms, separates freeze from kill, and redesigns around components with a lifetime.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A document-conversion app shelling out to native helpers saw random truncated outputs on Android 12 devices; the helpers were being killed as phantom processes.

questions.contextHtml: A document-scanning app (3M MAU, crash-free sessions 99.1 percent) embeds a third-party PDF/OCR library. Crashlytics attributes 0.8 percent of sessions to native crashes (SIGSEGV in libocr.so), mostly on malformed PDFs from email attachments, and 0.3 percent to OutOfMemoryError on 2 GB devices when decoding 40 MP pages. An engineer proposes running the library in android:process=":ocr". Another proposes android:isolatedProcess="true". The library needs the input file and returns a 200-page text result (about 3 MB).
questions.promptHtml: Do you adopt a separate process? Which kind, and how do you design the interface and failure handling?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Yes, separate process fixes crashes" with no mention of IPC limits, startup cost, or what happens when the process dies mid-call. Or "No, wrap it in try/catch", which cannot catch a native signal.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the library need app permissions, network, or the app's files? Is the input from an untrusted source? What latency budget per page? Is the library thread-safe? Why: decides isolated vs private process and the IPC design.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Validate and cap page size before decoding, downscale at decode (inSampleSize), reject malformed headers cheaply.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The native crash is a parsing bug on malformed input; the OOM is Java heap exhaustion from large bitmaps. A separate process fixes neither bug but converts a whole-app crash into a recoverable failure, and gives OCR its own heap budget.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce with the captured sample files; check tombstones and ApplicationExitInfo; compare dumpsys meminfo PSS in a prototype process; measure IPC cost with Perfetto.
  5. Root cause: An untrusted-input native library sharing an address space and heap with the UI.
  6. Fix (design): A bound service in an isolated process.
<service android:name=".OcrService"
    android:process=":ocr"
    android:isolatedProcess="true"
    android:exported="false"/>

isolatedProcess runs with no permissions and no access to the app's data, which fits untrusted parsing; it cannot use the network or app files, so pass input via ParcelFileDescriptor and return results through a pipe or a file descriptor, not a Bundle (the Binder transaction buffer is about 1 MB shared per process, so a 3 MB result in a Parcel would fail with TransactionTooLargeException; chunk 14). Handle DeadObjectException/onBindingDied: restart, mark the file as "unprocessable" after N failures, show a clear error. 7. Prevention: Fuzz the parser with corpus files, track proc_exit reasons for :ocr, run an instrumented test that kills :ocr mid-request, and a memory test on a 2 GB emulator. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Costs: extra process baseline memory (tens of MB, measure), IPC latency, lifecycle complexity, cold start of the process on first use (do it lazily and keep it warm by a bind from the scanning screen). Priority: the process is bound to the UI client, so it dies with the UI unless the work is long; if the user must continue in the background, use a foreground service. I would not move the whole app to multiple processes, and I would not use a global process name.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The library needs a license file in app storage. → Isolated process cannot read it; use a private :ocr process (not isolated) or pass the bytes via FD.
  • Results arrive page by page. → Stream through a pipe or a Messenger/callback per page instead of one big Parcel.
  • Crash loops on a poisoned file. → Persist a "poison" marker and skip the file next time.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A scanner team cut visible crashes from 0.8 percent to 0.05 percent by isolating the parser, and discovered the remaining failures were a bug in their own retry loop that kept re-sending a poisoned file.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests try/catch or any process without trade-offs.
  • Hire: Proposes a separate process with IPC and death handling.
  • Strong hire: Chooses isolated vs private deliberately, avoids the 1 MB Binder limit via FD streaming, quantifies memory/IPC costs, and plans poison-file handling.

questions.contextHtml: A messaging app (2M DAU) gets a product request: "The app must stay connected in the background so messages show up instantly. On our Pixel test phone it gets killed after about 5 minutes with the screen off." The current design keeps a WebSocket open in a plain Service started on app launch. Support tickets report delayed messages (median 4 min, p95 27 min) on Android 12+ devices, and battery complaints from the 15 percent of users whose OEM keeps the service alive. FCM is integrated but only used for marketing pushes. No further detail is given on what "instantly" means.
questions.promptHtml: How do you respond to this requirement, and what do you build?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make it a foreground service so it never dies", or "ask users to disable battery optimisation". It treats keeping a process alive as the goal rather than meeting a delivery SLA within platform rules and battery cost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is "instant": under 2 s or under 30 s? Does it apply to all users or only an active conversation? Is a visible ongoing notification acceptable? What is the battery budget? Do we have analytics on delivery latency? Why: turns a vague demand into a testable SLA.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Send message notifications through FCM high-priority data messages now, which wakes the app even in Doze, and fetch the payload on receipt. Stop the always-on socket for users in the background.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The plain service is stopped by background execution limits (Android 8+ stops background services shortly after the app leaves the foreground) or killed as a service-class process. (b) Doze/standby throttle network on the socket. (c) OEM kills. Red herring: server push latency.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce with screen off: adb shell dumpsys deviceidle force-idle, am set-standby-bucket; check exit reasons; look at dumpsys batterystats for wakelocks and wake-ups; measure FCM delivery latency end to end.
  5. Root cause: The architecture assumes a long-lived background process, which the platform explicitly does not offer to ordinary apps; delivery should be push-driven, with the app woken per message.
  6. Fix: Short-term: FCM high-priority messages for chat (priority guidance applies: it must result in a user-visible notification or the system may lower priority; verify FCM docs), with a quick sync on receipt via expedited work. Long-term: keep a socket only while the app is visible or during an active conversation. If product insists on a persistent connection for some users, evaluate a foreground service with a justified type; note the Play policy and Android 14/15 type and timeout rules (chunk 08), plus an ongoing notification and the battery cost: a socket with keepalive every 4 min wakes the radio 360 times a day.
class MsgService : FirebaseMessagingService() {
    override fun onMessageReceived(m: RemoteMessage) {
        val id = m.data["conversation"] ?: return
        WorkManager.getInstance(this).enqueueUniqueWork(
            "sync-$id", ExistingWorkPolicy.APPEND_OR_REPLACE,
            OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<SyncWorker>()
                .setExpedited(OutOfQuotaPolicy.RUN_AS_NON_EXPEDITED_WORK_REQUEST)
                .build()
        )
    }
}
  1. Prevention: Track message delivery latency p50/p95 by device/OEM/bucket, alert on regressions, and a lab test with Doze and rare bucket.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not ship a permanent foreground service for all users (battery, policy, user trust), would not add a boot receiver restart loop, would not tell users to disable optimisation as the default. I would offer an optional "reliable delivery" setting for opt-in users with a clear notification.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Users in China without Google services. → FCM is unavailable; use vendor push services or an opt-in foreground service, accepting the cost.
  • Product wants calls to ring instantly. → High-priority FCM with a full-screen intent/call style notification; a call in progress may legitimately use a foreground service (verify type and permission).
  • Android 15 FGS timeout. → Applies to some types; messaging socket FGS is not a good fit for dataSync (verify per release).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A chat team replaced its always-on service with push-plus-sync and cut median delay from 4 min to 2 s while battery complaints dropped by roughly a third; the PM's real requirement had been "no missed messages overnight".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Keeps the socket alive with a foreground service or battery-optimisation prompts.
  • Hire: Proposes FCM high-priority plus sync and explains why background services are limited.
  • Strong hire: Clarifies the SLA, quantifies battery cost, tests under Doze/standby, handles non-GMS, and keeps FGS as a justified exception.
